title: The Foreigner Among You
subtitle: The command to love the sojourner is binding. The policy for a just and ordered nation is contested. We are obligated to hold both.
question: Scripture commands the people of God to love the stranger, the ger, the one without papers or protection. Does that command settle the question of immigration policy, or does it leave faithful Christians arguing in good conscience about borders, law, and order?
whyItMatters: There is a kind of argument the church has learned to win by refusing to enter it. We pick the half of the truth that costs us nothing and call it the whole. On immigration both sides do this, and I have done it. I have used the word compassion to avoid the word law, and I have used the word law to avoid the face of a frightened family at a border I will never have to cross. The Bible does not let me keep either evasion.
biblicalFoundation:
The command arrives without softening. 'Love the sojourner, therefore, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt' (Deuteronomy 10:19). It is grounded not in sentiment but in memory. Israel is told to love the stranger because Israel was once the stranger, enslaved and unwelcome, and the God who heard them in Egypt now binds them to hear the cry of the foreigner among them. Leviticus 19:34 says it plainer still: the ger living among you shall be treated as the native-born, and you shall love him as yourself. This is not advice. It is the same construction used of the great command itself.

The oppression of the ger is named repeatedly as a sin that calls down judgment. 'You shall not wrong a sojourner or oppress him' (Exodus 22:21). The prophets indict the nation for it. To grind the face of the stranger is, in the prophetic mind, to forget who you are and Whose you are. And Israel never gets to graduate from this memory. Even settled in the land, the people are told that the land is not finally theirs: 'the land is mine, for you are strangers and sojourners with me' (Leviticus 25:23). The owner is a tenant. The native is a guest. This unsettles every claim of pure possession.

The New Testament does not relax the obligation. It deepens it and turns it on the reader. The Holy Family flees a murderous king and becomes a refugee household in Egypt, so that the Lord himself knows from the inside what it is to run for a child's life across a border. When a lawyer asks Jesus who his neighbor is, hoping to draw a line he can stay safely behind, Jesus answers with a Samaritan, a man of the wrong blood and the wrong worship, who crosses the ethnic line the priest would not cross. The point is not that the Samaritan had a policy. The point is that he stopped. And the harvest law of Leviticus 19 had already rehearsed this: do not reap to the very edges of your field, leave the gleanings for the poor and for the ger, build into your economy a deliberate margin where the outsider can be gathered in.

Peter then names the church itself with the old word. We are 'sojourners and exiles' (1 Peter 2:11), strangers on the earth, a people who hold no permanent citizenship here. The church that forgets it is a community of resident aliens will always find it easy to despise them.

churchRecord.led: When the church has remembered its own exile, it has opened its doors before it was asked. Congregations have housed refugees, sponsored families, sat in courtrooms with the undocumented, and run the quiet networks that fed and sheltered the stranger when the state would not. In its better hours the church has been the place where the foreigner found a name and a table.
churchRecord.failed: And the church has also baptized the hardness of its own tribe. It has read the command to love the sojourner and then voted, given, and spoken as though the foreigner were a threat to be managed rather than a neighbor to be loved. It has let national belonging masquerade as Christian conviction, and it has been silent while families were treated as case numbers. We did this. I did this.

whereWeAgree: Scripture does not leave this to preference. The command to love the stranger, to refuse to oppress the ger, and to care for the foreigner among us is binding on every Christian, and no appeal to order or nation cancels it.
captureLeft: The left can flatten the question until love means only open arms and any concern for law, security, or the limits of a community is recast as cruelty. It can wave away the real disorder, the strained towns, the exploited labor, and the genuine duties a nation owes its own poor, treating prudence itself as a sin and ending the conversation it claims to want.
captureRight: The right can take the legitimate language of order and law and use it as a respectable cover for a hardness the gospel forbids. Border becomes an idol, the stranger becomes a category, and 'they broke the law' becomes the verse that conveniently silences every verse about loving the one who is far off.
whereWeDiffer: How a just and ordered nation should set its laws, its limits, its enforcement, and its mercy is a prudential question, weighing real goods that pull against each other, and faithful Christians who share the binding command to love the stranger will land in different places on the policy. That difference is not the difference between obedience and disobedience.
theCost: To hold both truths is to lose the comfort of a side. You will be called soft by the people who want only walls and naive by the people who want only welcome. The prophetic word here cuts toward whoever is in the room. If you are sure your politics has already obeyed the command, you have probably not yet heard it. The cost is that the stranger has a face, and once you have seen it you cannot argue about him as if he were a number.
charge: Love the sojourner. That is settled, and it is not yours to soften. Then argue about the policy in good conscience and in fear, knowing the law you defend will be measured against the love you owe. Do not let your nation tell you whom to fear, and do not let your compassion excuse you from the hard work of a just order. The stranger and the prisoner are still at the gate. They were Christ in Egypt. They may be Christ at your border. You will not be asked what your policy was. You will be asked whether you stopped.
